utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us begin by seeking a clarification from you as to your submission late yesterday afternoon. Is it that the submissions made by this witness in his case should be admitted into evidence or that the newspaper articles that were shown to him as being written by Dulovic be admitted into evidence, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, as you may recall, I presented here the submission of Mr. Seselj which he submitted to the other side in connection with Dulovic and his testimony in which he challenges the truth of his statements. In this submission, he relied on the fact that in 1991, at the time of those events, Dulovic wrote a number of very positive articles about the events in Vukovar and then testified quite differently here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if it's the submission, we have already ruled that we are not admitting that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we're not prepared to reconsider that. But I thought you might also have been submitting that the articles, the newspaper articles, be admitted. That's another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You interrupted me before I finished what I was going to say. I certainly do tender those newspaper articles. They are a public document. They were published. But I asked you, Mr. Robinson, whether the tendering of those articles, which confirm what Mr. Seselj said in his submission, apart from being admitted into evidence, can also be a basis on which Mr. Seselj's submission could be admitted because he relied on those articles when compiling his submission. That's why I wanted you to reconsider admitting that submission. I therefore tender both the newspaper articles and at the same time ask you to reconsider whether the admission of those articles can be a basis for admitting the submission in which Mr. Seselj relies on those articles when presenting his claims about Dulovic in his submission to the opposite side. I think I've been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see you have been influenced by Mr. Nice's practice of applying for reconsideration. The Trial Chamber is not prepared to reconsider the admission of the submissions which we said was predominantly a matter of argument presented by Mr. Seselj to the other Trial Chamber. As to the other matter, the admission of the newspaper articles, we'll hear from Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, these newspaper articles were not, I think, put to the witness, we don't know what if anything he would say about them or their attribution to him. In those circumstances, it would not be appropriate, in our submission, for them to become exhibits in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they not put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think so. If they were -- if they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To Dulovic. I'm so sorry, yes. To Dulovic. If they were put, then I'm in error, but our recollection is not. He gave some summary evidence about what happened to his newspaper articles, but I don't think they were put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things you were going to check was whether you had been aware of these articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I was going to check that, I'm sorry I haven't done that. I think the position is this: The submission to which the witness and the accused have both referred was itself, I think, in Serbian, and the newspaper articles were, of course, in Serbian. In those circumstances, a decision was made to translate the article but not -- I beg your pardon, the submission but not the articles, and it hasn't been possible in -- it hasn't been done in the time since yesterday and today to see whether these were the particular articles we had or not. But even if we had had them, they haven't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know if the Dulovic articles were ever disclosed under Rule 68 as potentially exculpatory material or material that undermined the credibility of the witness. Maybe that is something the Prosecution should consider, if they did have a record of those articles, whether they were disclosed. The articles could become exhibits in the case and produced through a witness if they've been discovered later on as being contradictory to his testimony and published in a newspaper written by him and if he's given contradictory testimony here and there is a means of putting that into evidence, that is plainly so and it's a matter of weight and maybe the witness could be recalled to deal with such inconsistent statement. So this isn't evidence that is capable of being shut out for all time, in our submission, but maybe it should be considered whether they were ever disclosed under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can check that, but of course the first answer would be that this is open-source material and probably wouldn't be an obligation on us to disclose it in any event. But Mr. Saxon, who, as you know, has been dealing with Rule 68 disclosure, will check his records in the course of the morning, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the moment, we'll mark the document for identification pending translation and information as to whether it had been disclosed. That's a matter that we will take into consideration, not that it is conclusive or decisive by itself.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D305, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I assume you recall that a few days ago we tendered into evidence reports about the communiques issued by Goran Matic in the beginning of 2000 concerning the Spider group and their participation in Srebrenica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think the time has come to put this back on the ELMO and -- we have no time to put it on the ELMO, so did the spokesman of the government say that it was our duty towards the truth to establish what happened during the crimes in Srebrenica, and he said what the results were of the investigation carried out after the arrest of the Spider group. And in the investigation against the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... accused giving evidence, and is there a question coming out of all this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you recall that the government spokesman, on behalf of the government, says that the perpetrators of the crime in Srebrenica had been arrested? They were the commanders of the 10th Sabotage Detachment which shot prisoners of war in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was announced to the public, that Jugoslav Petrusic, Milorad Pelemis, and several other members of the so-called 10th Sabotage Detachment had been arrested. They had formed a new group called Pauk, Spider. Their aim was to organise an assassination of you, and they took a direct part in the shooting of Muslim prisoners of war near Srebrenica. This was stated to the public pursuant to investigations carried out by the courts and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Do you recall reading here the criminal report against Erdemovic, who has been tried here, in which it says that the shooting was carried out under orders of Milorad Pelemis, the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and the enumerated members of this detachment?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Erdemovic was also a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and as such he took part in the shootings. And we also have information that members of the 10th Sabotage Detachments were not just Serbs. They were also Croats, Muslims, and Slovenians, and there were quite a few foreigners among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My recollection is that this is ground that we have already covered. You have already dealt with this. I'm hearing this for the second time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I put this in order for us to establish whether the public on behalf of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was told who the perpetrators were and that they were in prison.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The public was told that the perpetrators of the crimes in Srebrenica had been found, they had been arrested, and that their guilt was proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did this communique include the information that they received 2 million German marks for what they did because they were mercenaries of foreign intelligence agencies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were paid by the French intelligence agencies, and they organised the sending of mercenaries from Republika Srpska to Congo to fight for French interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us put on the ELMO the decision I received in the meantime of the district court in Belgrade terminating the detention of Jugoslav Petrusic, Pelemis, and the others, those who ten months briefly had been named by the government as the perpetrators of the crime in Srebrenica, that is, the execution of prisoners of war. Could this please be put on the ELMO. Mr. Seselj, here in this decision, in line 5 already, after where it says "Decision," does it say that they were arrested pursuant to a decision of the investigating judge of the district court on the 14th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, they were arrested on the 11th of November, and so their detention is counted as of the 11th of November, and you can see that in the statement of reasons, in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, can we see here that for the acts for which the authorities had established that they had been committed by the 10th Sabotage Detachment for Srebrenica, which can be seen from Erdemovic's criminal report and from the statement made by Matic ten months prior to that, because Erdemovic was April 1996, from this can we see that they were not tried for that at all, nor is any mention made of the crime they committed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After the putsch of the 5th of October, 2000, the criminal proceedings against this group made up of Jugoslav Petrusic, Milorad Pelemis, Slobodan Orasanin, Branko Vlaco and Rade Petrovic, the proceedings were narrowed down to focus on crime and extortion, and they were all given sentences of one year in prison to cover the time they spent in detention. So what was done was to select the most lenient form of sentence and crime, and for that crime they received just one year imprisonment, all of them, and that was for extortion, which provides a sentence of up to ten years in prison, so they were given a minimum sentence of one year and then they were released, they were placed at liberty. And there was a complete cover-up of their participation in the execution of Muslim prisoners of war in Srebrenica which was established without any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, since you yourself were a participant in all the events, an active political participant in the events during those years and especially at the end of the year 2000, can you tell us how legality looked after the putsch on the 5th of October, in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle of legality and lawfulness in Serbia after the 5th of October, 2000, was completely abolished. It didn't exist. In Serbia in the years to come there was arbitrariness on the part of the Mafia and general tyranny. Political adversaries of the regime began to be persecuted. The authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is 2000 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is highly relevant, Mr. Robinson. The court could not even consider the most grievous crimes perpetrated by these perpetrators, and it was the public that informed the authorities ten months previously by the government spokesman for this scandal to go ahead and for them to release these people merely 40 days after the putsch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The newly established regime of Zoran Djindjic systematically covered up the massacre in Srebrenica and saved the main perpetrators involved in the massacre. All the courts were instrumentalised by the executive powers that be and adhered to their orders. The constitutional order was to all intents and purposes toppled, and the government and authorities even enacted retroactively tax laws and other laws to settle accounts with their adversaries. And they acted against anybody that was not like-minded, and had the support of the Western powers in doing that, to boot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to the best of your knowledge, what was the motive for covering up this -- for the cover-up of the crimes of the perpetrators, the direct perpetrators, the commanders and members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who, without any doubt as it was established, had carried out the execution of the prisoners of war in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the motives, I learnt about those motives at the time when I was vice-president or vice-premier of the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm quite happy to remind the Court of the impropriety of what this witness is being asked. It's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand the gist of the evidence is that some of the crimes in Srebrenica were committed by these people, and that may be relevant. The motives, however, for a cover-up we don't consider to be relevant. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have in mind that Drazen Erdemovic was tried here, a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and that Mr. Nice and his office are well aware of who perpetrated the crime in Srebrenica and that this is proof and evidence that Mr. Nice consciously and intentionally is avoiding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do not attribute motives to the -- ill-motives to the Prosecutor. You went astray last week. You're not to follow the same course. If you have a legal submission to make as to why we should hear the evidence, then make it. Why do you say we should hear this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely because of that, Mr. Robinson. Because Mr. Nice here quite recently, once again on several occasions, claimed that the authorities at the time that I was president and Mr. Seselj at the time vice-premier of the government, and his members, ministers of the federal government, covered up the Srebrenica case. Now, these documents show quite the contrary, that is to say that our government uncovered what it was all about. We arrested Erdemovic in 1996. You wouldn't have even taken him to trial here had we not arrested him, but you released him. And this Prosecution did not bring any lawsuit against those who perpetrated that particular crime; the entire 10th Sabotage Unit along with its commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've already heard that evidence. What else is there to it? We've already heard that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, apart from that, I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are moving into the area of non-forensic political comment, which will not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is not a political comment. It is a legal argument, the fact that here in this room Mr. Nice claimed that we covered up the crime in Srebrenica, whereas we can see quite the contrary here and quite the contrary is being proved here. Now I'd like to show an excerpt from a film that I received pursuant to Rule 68 from Mr. Nice a few months ago as disclosure. I think Obrad Stevanovic was testifying at the time but I didn't have time to show the tape then. I received it pursuant to Rule 68 from the opposite side over there. It's a brief excerpt from the film - may we have it played - and it speaks about the background.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let me tell you that there was an error in the technical booth. I've been informed that Mr. Ognjanovic is putting that error right. I wanted to show a different excerpt. This is a very long film, what we're seeing now, but it's not the right part of it, the right excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you saying that the five minutes that we just spent watching this film has been wasted? Why didn't you stop us earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept expecting the excerpt that I wanted to show you to start. I don't have either the time or the possibility to watch these films in the -- in prison, and my associates prepared this, and I was told that they had prepared the exact portion and extract I wished to show here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have the correct excerpt now for us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the minutes and time. I should have. Now I've just been told that they're trying to put that mistake right. I would like you to hear the statement by the Muslim official from Srebrenica with regard to the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "We are now part, working for the peace to make a peace, to -- to reach an agreement about a peaceful solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but one point is very important. It's a problem of guarantee for -- guarantee for the agreement. We will -- we will ask and request from the President Clinton that United States participate in -- in this [indiscernible]. Of course, within NATO forces and so on." "Some surviving members of the Srebrenica delegation have stated that President Izetbegovic also told them that he had learned that a NATO intervention in Bosnia and Herzegovina was possible, but could only occur if the Serbs were to break into Srebrenica ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we don't need to see this any further. We can stop the tape there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What is the question that you have to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I do ask the question, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that the quotation which supports the assertions, the claims, of the Muslim head from Srebrenica is to be found in the report of the UN Secretary-General dated the 15th of November, 1999, and I have that report here before me. It is on page 31, paragraph 115. You will be able to find the quotation that you just saw, among other things. I don't know whether you want -- would like me to have it placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I would like is a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did you have any knowledge about the political background of the events in Srebrenica in the light of all these facts that I have presented here from Erdemovic's criminal report, his arrest, the participation of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, Izetbegovic's political calculations with Clinton and the events that were to follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, that kind of question is an invitation for a very long and meandering answer from the witness. Put --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put a more focused and specific question to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you've just seen a film now. Before that, you saw those press releases and you know the press release about what happened in Srebrenica. Your own representatives were on that government. You know about Erdemovic and his conviction here, and you've just seen this film. Do you know about what you've just seen on this film?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbia, on a few occasions I received intelligence reports, both from the military and the civilian security service, that is to say the state security service, which contained concrete data that our services had obtained, namely that it was foreigners who had initiated the crime in Srebrenica, that the foreigners organised everything, that it was not hard to find the actual executors among the mercenaries but the objective was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I interrupt briefly. Who had organised the crime in Srebrenica, you mention. Now, could you define that crime for me before we go any further? Can you tell me how many victims there were of the crime you say was organised by foreign forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying that the French intelligence service directly organised this in concert with other Western intelligence agencies, and according to the information that I received then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 1.200 victims we've been speaking about earlier in the evidence or are we now talking about a larger number of victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're going back over the same territory that we've already been over. Is that the position? We've been over the French influence, we've been over the mercenaries, we've been over the individuals who were involved, we've been over Erdemovic. Are we going over it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, that quite simply is not correct. I am not talking about the same thing again but you simply don't want to hear me out. Please give me two or three minutes to say what I've got to say. If that is repetition, then interrupt me. According to intelligence reports, we found out that everything had been staged for several reasons. First of all, to serve as a basis for issuing an indictment in The Hague against Radovan Karadzic in order to eliminate Karadzic from the forthcoming negotiating process. Secondly, because Western politicians on several occasions made unwise statements to the effect that there was a genocide going on against the Muslims in Bosnia, at all costs they wanted to construe at least something that would be akin to genocide, and the key deception that they created was an inversion of categories; a protected zone of the United Nations and a protected group according to the Genocide Convention. According to the Genocide Convention, it was only the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Muslims as a whole that could have been a protected category. According to the 1991 census, there was 2.160.000 of them, and the protected zone from Srebrenica -- of Srebrenica was a safe area of the United Nations. That category has nothing to do with the Convention on Genocide. So that was the deception; namely that the Muslims of Srebrenica be proclaimed a protected group according to the Convention on Genocide, to abuse the name of a protected area by equating it to the category of a protected group, and that that be used for levelling an accusation against the Serbs that they had committed genocide. Then the Office of the Prosecutor in The Hague was instructed to act accordingly by their masters from the West. That is the deception. I as vice-premier received detailed information from our services about this deception, to exaggerate the number of victims as much as possible, that all the Muslim casualties from 1992 to 1995 be put onto one list as if they had all been executed after the liberation of Srebrenica, that all of those who got killed in any way be placed on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did you have occasion to read the testimony of General Morillon before the French parliament in which he says that the reason for Srebrenica was a reason of state and that it should be sought on the line Paris-New York?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had that document in my hands as vice-president -- as vice-premier of the Republic of Serbia, and that is additional proof that the crime in Srebrenica was construed by the West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in his hearing before the French parliament Morillon said that this was a trap for Mladic but that for reasons of state this had to be done to him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that this was a trap for Mladic. Morillon, in the French parliament, stated that this was a trap for Mladic, but he kept silent about the fact that this was first and foremost a trap for Karadzic, to eliminate Karadzic, and that the crime in Srebrenica should be used as a pretext for the systematic mass bombing of Republika Srpska which had rendered the Serb army so incapable that it made it possible to launch a major Croat-Muslim offensive and to involve directly the army of Croatia into that initiative.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please pause before the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter is asking you to pause before you put your question. And the same for Mr. Seselj before he answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you have any knowledge that would give you and through which you could give an explanation to the fact that these perpetrators from the 10th Sabotage Detachment were not held accountable here where Srebrenica is referred to to such a large degree?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As vice-president of the government of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That explanation not going to be helpful. Ask another question. Mr. Milosevic, you had indicated that you would have completed your examination-in-chief by yesterday. We're here this morning. In the past you have always tried to conclude with a flourish, and that flourish usually gets you into trouble. You ask leading questions, and you descend into political comment. If you do not have any other questions to put to the witness, then end your examination-in-chief or I will end it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have just completed my examination, but you interrupted me and therefore I haven't thanked Mr. Seselj for his evidence yet. I have provided documents here which primarily have to do with the allegations made by Mr. Nice to the effect that the authorities of Serbia and Yugoslavia were trying to cover up what happened in Srebrenica, whereas documents prove the contrary. Before Mr. Nice starts examining Mr. Seselj, I ask you to admit into evidence a letter that was on the ELMO that Mr. Seselj read or, rather, he read excerpts. The 8th of December, 1992. This was a letter written by Radovan Karadzic to the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Mrs. Sadako Ogata, and to the head of the ICRC, Mr. Sommaruga, with copies to Lord Owen and Dobrica Cosic, president of Yugoslavia, and it shows that there was agreement among all three warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely the Serb, Croat, and Muslim side, under the auspices of the UN in Geneva, to allow the civilians who wished to leave the territory under the control of one side to cross over to the territory held by another side, that they should be allowed to do so. This confirms the statements made by the witness during his testimony about the departure of civilians from a particular territory to another territory that was under the control of a side they considered to be friendly. So according to the agreement reached among the three parties in Geneva, that was feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is this letter, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fortunately, I have it both in the Serbian and English languages. Please have a look at the Serb copy and the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This was actually put to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was put to Mr. Seselj in relation to his testimony about that, namely that major movements of population from one area to another were not a consequence of any kind of ethnic cleansing but rather an agreement reached by the three sides to have this organised and to ensure the support of the Red Cross and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it was put, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. Please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D306.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I have no further questions. Mr. Robinson, I also ask that this decision of the district court from Belgrade dated the 13th of November, 2000, releasing those persons from prison, also be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D307.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As it's not translated, it will, in accordance with the practice, be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have two questions, Mr. Milosevic. You referred to a report of the United Nations Secretary-General of the 15th of November, 1999. Is that already an exhibit in the case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it is but I'm not sure of that. I assume that the relevant reports pertaining to Yugoslavia are all exhibits in this case. I have the report here in front of me, and I can loan it to you so that you can at least cast a glance at it, because the report that I got on the basis of Rule 68 as part of the exculpatory material includes what I highlighted here, number 31. I used yellow highlighter. It's a very long report, over 100 pages. You can have a look. The report is entitled The Fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to see the part that you've highlighted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. The second part of the highlighted paragraph is the one you could have seen on the overhead projector as it was quoted by the Dutch too. It pertained to the killing of 5.000 persons. The highlighted section, the one highlighted in yellow - and could you have it enlarged so that it can be read - you saw this on the film, part of it. "[In English] Some surviving members of the Srebrenica delegation have stated that President Izetbegovic also told them he had learned that a NATO intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina was possible, but could only occur if the Serbs were to break into Srebrenica, killing at least 5.000 of its people." [Interpretation] That's what you saw on the screen. And that is an integral part of the report of the Secretary-General dated the 15th of November, 1999. Also on the screen you could see the chief of police from Srebrenica, a Muslim, saying that Izetbegovic had told them that Clinton had proposed to them that they kill some Muslims so that there could be an intervention afterwards. That was what he said on camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've perhaps misunderstood. I thought you were claiming that there was some support in this report for the idea that this was all being staged, but all this does is reflect the assertion which is then denied. Now, is there another passage that you were going to refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I've just presented this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The second matter is this: You put into Mr. Seselj's mouth various words said to have been uttered by General Morillon before the French parliament. Do you have a transcript of what he said to the French parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do. It's a public document, the hearing of General Morillon before the French parliament. As a matter of fact, I think I've already exhibited it here, but I'm going to ask my associates to find a copy and to have it handed over to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The report on The Fall of Srebrenica is Exhibit 547, tab 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the UN report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what about the video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the video, too. By all means I would like to have it admitted into evidence. According to Rule 68, I received it, so both parties agreed that it is important, otherwise Mr. Nice would not have sent that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a Dutch programme. Do you know the name of the programme?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can look it up, and I can tell you the name of the programme, of the whole programme, that is. It is a Dutch programme because it was their soldiers who were in Srebrenica at the material time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have something to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that something is provided to the accused under Rule 68 doesn't make it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. That's not the basis under which we're admitting it, I assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- a television programme, and as to television programmes, we've been permitted to put in a very limited number of excerpts from particular television programmes when the witness concerned has been able to say something specific about the passage seen. I'm not sure that that is the case here. This is just a general television programme. It's up to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit only those parts that were played.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D308.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, before we move from Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, let's understand one another. I didn't ask for the entire tape to be admitted into evidence but only the portions I played. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move from Srebrenica, let's see if I can understand a few things you've been saying. What do you mean "staged"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean by that is that the French intelligence service, through its agents, paid the 10th Sabotage Detachment and its members to organise the shooting of Muslim prisoners of war near Srebrenica in order to ascribe this crime to the entire Serb leadership. That's what I mean when I say it was staged. There is no doubt that the crime actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the total numbers killed, as you know, the Krstic judgement says probably between 6 and 7.000, a figure adopted in the RS by their commission in a recent -- sorry, 7 to 8.000 in Krstic, a figure adopted by the RS in their comparatively recent concession about the massacre in Srebrenica. Are you saying that there were no other people killed apart from the 1.000 or 1.200 killed by the Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that it was not 7.000 who were killed. As far as I know, the Republika Srpska and its commission speak of 7.000 missing, not killed. I know for certain that on the list of those killed there are names of people who died much earlier. The list of those killed even includes names of Muslims who were arrested by Djukanovic's police in Montenegro and delivered to Deronjic in 1990, and he shot them then at that time. I cannot swear that only 1.200 were killed. It might have been a little more or a little less, but it is certainly not possible that 7.000 were executed. You are saying it was 7.000 in order to artificially construct a thesis that this was genocide, because according to the convention --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have responded to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the next thing is this: You speak of foreigners who staged this, foreigners about whom you learnt things from intelligence. Is this just the French or is it other nationalities that are involved as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The French intelligence service, according to the information of our intelligence services, carried this out. In their reports, our intelligence services - and I had these reports in my hands and read them - considered that the French had done this in agreement with other Western services, bearing in mind primarily the American intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That brings me to my next question: When was it that you had these reports in your hand?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sometime in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who made them available to you in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the deputy Prime Minister of Serbia, I regularly, almost daily, in the cabinet of the Prime Minister read various intelligence reports. There was one copy sent for the entire cabinet. It could not be photocopied or taken out of the Prime Minister's office. It could be read by the Prime Minister and the deputy Prime Ministers. Then it was taken away. It was registered under a number as a state secret. This can be confirmed by Mirko Marjanovic, the then Prime Minister, and as far as I know, all the four deputy Prime Ministers, at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have already had exhibited here an annual report or compilation of intelligence reports that seemed to be compiled by the Serbian government, and I think the point was that it openly recorded the information that was being obtained through intelligence. That evidence related to Kosovo rather than to any other part of Serbia, I think. But are you saying that there would be available a similar document which would be a compilation of intelligence reports in general relevant to the period of the war in Croatia -- sorry, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot speak of a whole document that might be a compilation of various reports from various periods of time. I am now speaking of daily or periodic reports which I was given access to either in the state security service or the military security service. They sent those to the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you think these reports are still available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could I know? I've been in prison for two and a half years. I don't know what has happened in Serbia in the meantime. It's up to you to ascertain that. But I can prove through the testimony of the then Prime Minister or my colleagues the other deputy Prime Ministers that these documents did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, His Honour brings me indeed to the point that I was interested in, but let's approach it in a slightly different way. You saw these documents in 1998. What exactly were they? We -- let me just help you a little bit. We've had the reports of the kind His Honour Judge Bonomy has told you about, we've had quite a lot of intercepts of people speaking to one another. Those are two of the sorts of raw material that we may have from intelligence sources. Now you tell us, Mr. Seselj, precisely what category of material were you reviewing in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were documents that the intelligence services delivered for their inspection to the highest ranking government officials. I have mentioned one of those documents pursuant to which we replaced Jovica Stanisic, and later on Mr. Milosevic replaced Perisic. This was a whole file full of various intelligence documents about the CIA centre in Vienna who had the operational task of toppling Slobodan Milosevic. This includes information of opposition leaders from Serbia going for talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're an educated man. If you're given a report on an interesting or controversial topic, you'll be likely to want to know how reliable it is, what its sources are. Can you tell us, please, either in detail what the material was you reviewed or, if you can't remember, on what sources, what primary sources this material relied so that we can know what existed in the archives?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sources were under code, and we were not told about the specific sources, but I made an effort to check the content of these reports in other ways. Let me illustrate this in another way also. This information which I received as deputy Prime Minister in 2000 led me to name those who participated in the murder of Arkan in 2000. My information was of such a nature, and sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have a tendency to deviate from the subject. I think Mr. Nice wants to know what the sources were for the information about Srebrenica, not about Arkan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you about the nature of the information that was made available to me. It was made available to me for inspection, but I was quite clear about the sources. The sources mentioned were under code. The code usually had some kind of made-up name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the -- that's the intelligence -- that's the human intelligence source, perhaps. Now, in intelligence reporting, the human intelligence source may be disguised even from privileged readers like yourself by the intelligence services, but what he's reporting or she's reporting on doesn't need to be protected, so that if your human intelligence source says Mr. X and Madam Y made an agreement whereby Srebrenica would be staged, you the reader should be able to know who Mr. X and Madam Y were. Could you tell us, please, from your reading of the material if there are any individuals identified in this staging.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were reports I read about seven years ago. I cannot recall every detail. I recall the essence, and I recall the form in which these reports were made available to us. These reports concerned the most varied topics, but pursuant to the reports on Srebrenica, I did speak out in public later on. I was among the first in Serbia to publicly name one of the officers who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was the officer?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I publicly named on more than one occasion Colonel Beara, and that is common knowledge. You can find a large number of media reports on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, though, is about the individuals who were behind the cover-up. Beara, I presume, you indict as someone who implements it, but this is such an important matter, albeit seven years may have elapsed, one would expect you to remember individuals. Indeed, I would have expected you to speak out against them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On more than one occasion I did speak out against them. I condemned them in public. That is those criminals who executed Muslim prisoners of war in Srebrenica. There is evidence to show this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are looking behind that, for the French people who are supposed to be behind it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should I know who the French people were? Mr. Bonomy, here you are used to false witnesses brought by the Office of the Prosecutor who, even after a lapse of 15 years, recall every detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, it strikes me that that sort of assertion in response to the what I thought was measured debate we were having is bluff and demonstrates a failure on your part to address the issue which I'm seriously trying to address at the moment. However, no doubt Mr. Nice will be able to succeed where I have failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can only do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, Mr. Seselj, when and where you -- I haven't -- I haven't finished --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I protest against what you have said, that I'm bluffing. You as a Judge cannot permit yourself to say something like that. You can decide on that when I have finished my testimony. You cannot tell me here to my face that I am bluffing without any arguments to support it. That is not fitting for a Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the comment you made was that I was used to false witnesses brought by the Office of the Prosecutor who, even after a lapse of 15 years, recall every detail. Now, that's just an assertion, a generalisation which has no substance in its context because we are not dealing with, at the moment, witnesses who come here 15 years later. We're dealing with a witness of distinctive intelligence who has a close interest in Srebrenica, and it's against that background that I am asking the questions I'm asking. And to refer in the way you have to Prosecution witnesses with that sort of generalisation is pointless in the context of our debate, and for that reason I call it bluff. It's something that you assert with a view to concealing, perhaps, we'll have to investigate that later, your own absence of knowledge on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, when and where did you first set out the version of events that you told us about half an hour ago involving the staging of Srebrenica? Where did you first, and when, did you first set that out? In a speech, in a book, in an article, in an interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall when was the first time, but more than once I publicly stated that the execution of Muslim prisoners of war in Srebrenica was staged, and you have an abundance of testimony about that in my books, because in my books I publish my features, my television broadcasts, and my newspaper interviews. You have this available and there is an abundance of that. I didn't say it just once, I said it dozens of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, they're your books and I'd like you please to point us now, or after the first break if that's more convenient, to either the first, if you can, or at any event an early account by you that matches the account of staging that you gave to the Judges a little earlier. Now, can you give me that detail now or will you require the short break to search your memory and help us?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need any break. This is in my books. The Serbian public, all of it, is familiar with that. It's well known in the Serbian public that I have already spoken about this, but for me to look it up, I'm not your clerk, Mr. Nice. I abide by what I say, but it doesn't cross my mind to try and convince you of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm asking you to help the Judges, please, by referring us to a printed version, as you say it will be, of a first or early occasion when you gave this account. Will you give them that assistance?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will refer the Judges to my books which contain my television, radio, and newspaper interviews from 1997 and 1998 onwards. These books are full of statements of this kind, giving the version I am advocating here today based on the information available to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- what is wrong with Mr. Nice's suggestion that at the break, or even tonight, you might consider the position further and tell us when was actually the first time you spoke out about this? It seems a perfectly reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he wants to burden me with a lot of work outside this courtroom. I have submitted 80 books to the Office of the Prosecutor. My collected works are now being published in hardback, and do you want me to leaf through all of that? No. It's Mr. Nice's service that should do that. And then if they fail to find it they can say it's not there, and then I can try and catch out Mr. Nice and prove that he's lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I must say I'm concerned about this. We all have busy lives, Mr. Seselj, and you'll appreciate that the life of a Judge in this case is a busy one. It would just seem to be reasonable to ask the person who wrote the material to identify when he first referred to it, but if you cannot help, then the matter will have to rest there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will, of course, be as interventionist as is necessary with this witness to control him and to stop his excesses, but will the Court please look at the last line of the last answer. Bear in mind the character of some of the questioning of the accused last week, and I wonder if it would consider --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you protesting? Mr. Nice is on his feet. Let Mr. Nice address me first and then I'll hear from you. Mr. Nice, what is it that you're bringing to our attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm bringing to your attention the sort of observation that the witness has made, twinning it with the sort of questions and observations that the accused made last week, and I'm inviting the Chamber to ensure that an appropriate decorum is maintained in this Court. The last answer of this witness, and the last sentence of it, is absolutely improper and unacceptable and I'm not going to stand here endlessly while ill-disciplined accused or witnesses are given free rein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it's not -- the suggestion that you made that Mr. Nice might be proved to be lying is an inappropriate one and not acceptable. It's a remark I made to the accused as well. Mr. Nice is right; we must observe a level of decorum appropriate with the proceedings. Let us have mutual respect from all parties in the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to hear from you, Mr. Milosevic, on this. Mr. Seselj, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you are putting in my mouth something I did not say. I did not say that Mr. Nice was lying. I didn't say that once. What I said was that if Mr. Nice were to say that this was not contained in my books from that time, then I would bring my books here and I would catch him out and show he was lying. That was a conditional clause. I didn't say he was lying. There have been no excesses here, but he is now trying to create an incident. That, however, is his problem and your problem with him, not with me. I am trying to behave properly here and politely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on. Let us move on. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the last question I really want to ask you about this intelligence that you read, or the last subtopic on the intelligence you read, at least at the moment, is this: What was the date of that original intelligence? Was it 1995, 1996, or when?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date was a day before I read it. Therefore -- well, these reports were daily and periodic reports. The periodic reports sometimes contained analyses of certain topics and could then include information from previous years. However, every report that I read was dated from the previous day. Mr. Milosevic received the same kind of reports, as did a certain other number of people in the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The raw material upon which these reports was based, was that a 1998 conversation between perhaps a human intelligence source and someone else or a 1998 intercept looking back over three years, or was the raw material itself 1995 or 1996 material?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is simply an impossible question. How can I answer it? Who in my place could give a convincing answer to such a question? Our intelligence services had their people in various institutions in Serbia. They also had their people in the opposition political parties. They had their people abroad. An officer of the French army, during the NATO bombing, was shown to be a Serbian intelligence agent. Traditionally, our intelligence agencies were always very capable in that respect until the change in government in 2005, but you are now asking me to tell you about these reports in detail as if I had them before me now or as if I tried to memorise them at the time and learn them off by heart. I'm telling you about the basic facts I learned in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first mention this material to this accused? I don't want to know what you said to him, but in the proofing sessions when did you first mention the existence of this material to this accused?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we didn't even discuss this during the proofing sessions, but we did discuss it before or, rather, we discussed the crime in Srebrenica before on various occasions. When I was deputy Prime Minister, I frequently had consultations with Mr. Milosevic who was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We were coalition partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You would both have known of this material. I just want to know, do you know whether any effort has been made on behalf of the accused to produce this material to this Court?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. What the fate of that material is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... believe, if your account of it is accurate, that the material that you returned to its custodian has since been destroyed, is there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fate of the material is something that I do not know. All I can do is to draw your attention to the fact that after the 5th of October there was a lot of burning of various intelligence material and dossiers in the institute in Belgrade -- security in Belgrade. So what happened, I don't know. And I'm not -- I don't interfere with the work of the Defence team of Mr. Milosevic. All I'm doing is speaking about what I know. And what I say I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Courts will not be surprised to know that requests for assistance to produce documents that would have incorporated such material have of course been sent, and indeed followed up, but all with negative result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you, too, have to observe the pause. If you look, you'll see that you're overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I do continue, can Mr. Saxon bring you up-to-date with our inquiries into the proposed exhibit of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. The newspaper articles published in Politika by Jovan Dulovic were not attached to submission number 55 of Vojislav Seselj, which was provided to the Prosecution some months ago. These articles were merely referred to within the text of the submissions. Selected portions of these articles were referred to from pages 10 through pages 44 of Mr. Seselj's submission number 55. So at this time, the Prosecution does not have full copies of these articles in its possession. It has previously, in May of 2002, disclosed under Rule 66(B) other articles by Jovan Dulovic, the journalist, but these are different articles that were published in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I hope to return to Srebrenica as a topic if time allows later. However, there's one thing I want to ask you about and give you a chance to consider over the next day or so that I'll be asking you questions so that you can help us, and it relates to what you said about the proceedings against Erdemovic in 1996. Are you aware of the fact that Erdemovic had been interviewed by and had given an account of events to a journalist by the name of Janekovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, and that really was quite some years ago, this statement given by Erdemovic to a journalist led to his arrest in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was a pretext for his arrest in Serbia, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Janekovic's records of the interview were taken from the journalist at an airport, seized from, I think it's his or her luggage -- it's her luggage. Are you aware of that? Seized by the authorities from her luggage on the 2nd of March of 1996.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What I want you to help us with is this: Can you point us, please, to any public acknowledgement or public process against Erdemovic or anyone else in respect of Srebrenica before that date, the 2nd of March, 1996, when it was known that the journalist was in a position to reveal what Erdemovic had himself revealed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me questions on the basis of my negative answer to the previous question. I don't know that anybody seized any notes of any journalist. To the best of my recollections, Erdemovic was the first whom the authorities in Serbia prosecuted for Srebrenica, and that was just one year after the event in Srebrenica, or less than a year. And I was in the opposition at the time, I wasn't in the government at the time, so I can't give you any more detailed information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've answered questions about everything, you've claimed knowledge of nearly everything on all theatres of the conflicts and all matters of government and all matters of legal process, and I'm giving you a chance, the longest chance I can give you, to identify between now and the end of your testimony any public acknowledgement or public process by the authorities in Serbia of Erdemovic or of anyone else before the 2nd of March of 1996. I want your help on that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information that somebody before March 1996 publicly process -- was publicly processed because of the crime in Srebrenica. Now, as far as your comment goes that I said that I know everything, no. That's what the Trial Chamber said, and then semi-jokingly I confirmed that. I never said that I knew everything, was omniscient, nor can anybody be. Only God knows everything, and I am much lower down on that scale, but more than you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a few questions to ask you about your approach to this Tribunal, the relevance of which will become obvious, but first of all the question. Do you recognise the ICTY generally? Not this particular Chamber, we'll have no personalisation of this Chamber. Do you recognise the ICTY generally as a lawfully constituted body? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I consider that this International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia is unlawful, that it was established by an unlawful organ, the Security Council, which pursuant -- which, pursuant to the UN Charter, did not have the right to do so and that this Court was not established to establish justice but peace, and it is the first Court or Tribunal in the history of mankind given the task of establishing peace and not establishing the truth, justice. And as a legal man myself, as a professor of constitutional law, theoretically speaking I bring into question the legality and lawfulness of this Tribunal and I claim that it is not legal or lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again with no reference to the Judges in this particular Chamber, just to confirm what your position is about recognising the lawful authority of the judiciary of the Tribunal generally. Do you recognise any lawful authority in the judiciary generally?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that this Tribunal is not a lawful organ, that this Tribunal is anti-Serbian. It is a political institution as such, and this Tribunal is oriented against the interests of the Serb people. And the sources of financing fully compromise the Tribunal. It was not financed only by the United Nations but by Soros and many other private persons and states in the world who had a personal vested interest in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, at this stage I have to ask you about the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, when you came into this room, you took the solemn declaration. In what way, then, in light of your last two answers, does that bind you at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I solemnly declared before the eyes of the public and mankind that I will speak the truth without entering on that occasion to the fact of whether this Tribunal was lawful or unlawful, and I have adhered to that, to tell the truth. And -- however, I will always question the legality and lawfulness of this Tribunal, both professionally and on scientific grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So there's nothing in your declaration that binds you to the Court generally, or indeed to this Chamber specifically. As you've expressed it, it's to mankind; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have here the text of the declaration that I uttered and I declared here. "I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." I did not say here that I would recognise this Tribunal, which I consider to be illegal, that I would recognise the way in which it was established, and that I would recognise the alleged objectivity or unbiasedness because I claim that the Tribunal is biased and prejudiced, but what I did declare is something that was written down on this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a practical problem. One of the reasons I'm asking you these questions, and I'm only going to ask you a few but only a few more about your attitude to the Tribunal. If it ever becomes necessary or desirable for me in cross-examining you to refer to, in private session, of course, to witnesses who might be protected, is there any way you can explain to us that you would honour that protection and not publish their names?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since I arrived at The Hague prison, I did not disclose a single name of any protected witness, and I abide strictly by that provision because I don't want to put -- give you this argument of telling me that you're not informing me about the protected witnesses so that I can question their testimony. I never published -- made public their names except my Defence -- to my Defence team, and I did so to them legally. I sent them confidential material disclosed to me by the Prosecution, and they never made that public, they never published that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may have to return to that and just a few questions about your attitude before we move on to something else so that we can understand where you stand. Have you described -- and I haven't got a copy of this but you'll recollect words to this effect: Have you described to the BBC that The Hague is a place where there is an "anti-Serb plot" that you will unmask?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in the trial against me, I will unmask that anti-Serb plot by proving that all the accusations against me are false, based on false witnesses, based on false evidence, and politically motivated. Your motive was to do away with me from Serbian political life because there was the danger of my party taking over power in Serbia. So that is the sole reason for which you raised the indictment against me. You first raised the indictment and only then began to collect evidence against me. You had nothing against me once you raised the indictment, and you have nothing against me today either, and that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look at the following document, please, that I'm afraid is not translated, but nevertheless it's very short and you can help us with it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to provide me with documents in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes from your own website, so it is in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This lists some of the documents and books currently being advertised on your website; is that correct? Well, the Radical Party's website, your party's website.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just looking down that list of contemporary publications, is one headed A Genocidal Israeli Diplomat, Theodore Meron?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my book entitled The Genocidal Israeli Diplomat, Theodor Meron, because he was the Israeli foreign minister, and he implemented genocide against the Palestinian people and as such he cannot be qualified to be the president of the International Tribunal which is to try other people for similar crimes. And he abused his position as president of the Tribunal; he held a speech at the anniversary of Srebrenica and spoke about genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sometimes the answer can be very brief. If you feel it's going to be helpful for you to go on at length in the way you have done, I won't necessarily stop you, but the answer can be brief. Is a second --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if the answer is too brief, then it is not complete and not in the interests of justice for me to give incomplete answers. As you can see, all my answers follow the same direction as do your questions, and I'm just confirming what you've said. I'm answering in the affirmative, so you don't have to run away from my answers, and I'm doing my best to make them concise, well-centred, and concentrated on what you're asking me, but, of course, complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second book title that we see there, In the Jaws of the Whore Carla Del Ponte. Is that the sort of material your website is publishing? Yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I published a book under the title In the Jaws of the Whore Del Ponte. "Carla" and "Kurva" is a play on words. "Kurva," in the Serbian language, means prostitute, so the symbolism there is clear. I consider Carla Del Ponte in the legal sense to be a prostitute because she does not adhere to legal principles. She is downtreading them. She is waging an anti-Serb policy and wishes to try the whole Serbian people and makes a selection of the individuals whom she indicts in this Tribunal on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not going to stop there, Mr. Nice, I assume. I thought you would go through all the titles so I could explain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it -- this document comes from your magazine. I may have to find the passage, but there's a passage that's been translated into English, and on the Serbian version it's on the right-hand side of the page. And in February of this year, were you publishing in your magazine in respect of this Court an article headed The Criminals Are Banning Vucic's Visit? And in the second -- or the third paragraph, you say this: "Aleksandar Vucic is not coming to visit me in his capacity as a member of the Serbian Radical Party but rather as my accepted legal advisor. I accepted him as my legal advisor but you, all you members of The Hague Tribunal Registry -" perhaps you'd like to read the last line of that, please, to us, in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why didn't you read it all out? You read more beautifully than I do. At the end I said: "... all you members of the Registry office of The Hague Tribunal can only suck my dick." But that is not my article. It is my submission to the secretariat of The Hague Tribunal, which for a full two and a half years is preventing my Defence and refusing to register my legal advisors and in other ways violating elemental rules and regulations with regard to my status and rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Read the last short paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't do only the last one. I have to do the penultimate one and the last paragraph together because you can understand the last one only if I read the one but last paragraph as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "My legal advisors are not my Defence counsel and that is why they need not fulfil the conditions stipulated by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence for Defence counsel. All they have to do is to fulfil those conditions which I prescribe for them. And you can go on hampering my Defence and then ultimately you're going to have to eat all the shit that you excreted. "Fuck you all, beginning with Hans Holthuis, and so on, including that Tjarda van der Spoel, who is a crook." So that has nothing to do with my Defence. That's the man, and his aim is to make my Defence impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more and then I'm done with this. The next one, please, is an extract from your magazine or newspaper of April 2005. Could you just look at that. Perhaps the usher can even show the two pictures on the overhead projector. The first deals with -- the picture deals with the Pope, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it accuses the Pope of being the main culprit for the -- this is the late Pope, the main culprit for the crimes falsely alleged against yourself. Can you, in a couple of sentences so that we can understand it, and I would ask you to be brief, explain why it is that you say the late Pope was responsible for the crimes charged against you? You dealt with it in evidence and I didn't follow it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: John Paul II, the Pope until the recent one, continued the traditional Vatican anti-Serb policy, and he is the main culprit for all the crimes in this war, because through his policy he caused the war. And I have a multitude of evidence. My legal advisors are busy preparing an extensive report on it, because the crux of my Defence is the thesis that for all the crimes that are being ascribed to me, the main culprit for those are Pope John Paul II. And let me remind you of The Book of Recollections by the American ambassador to the Vatican written at the beginning of the 1990s about the papal policy and his efforts to break up Yugoslavia, and that is the thesis that I will be promoting, so be well prepared when my trial goes ahead, that will be the main thesis of my Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You haven't produced any documentation to support this as part of your evidence here. Just help us, please: Do you have any piece of material, any bit of writing or any recorded intercept or piece of intelligence that connects directly to the late Pope whom you have associated with this policy? Any piece of paper you'd like to produce to us?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a book, A Book of Recollections, written by the American ambassador to the Vatican at the beginning of the 1990s which was published in Zagreb as well, and my legal advisors are busy writing an extensive report which will be finished by the New Year on that subject, and I'm going to disclose it to you, to hand it over pursuant to Rule 67 of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure in preparation for my Defence. The Pope was the first to recognise the independence of Croatia before any other country did, in an unlawful way, and that is how he opened the dam and the flow was from the other Western countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how much more of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only one more point and then I'll be moving on, but I'm going to explain a little more the significance of what I've been asking in my next few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just turn over, please, the next page in the article. There's a caricature or cartoon of Ms. Del Ponte and "Arbeit Macht Frei." Before I ask you a question about this, you made a point of volunteering to come to this Tribunal, didn't you, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, consciously and voluntarily. That's how I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having done that, having voluntarily submitted yourself to the authorities whether you recognise --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't surrender. I didn't surrender to any authorities. As soon as I heard that there was an indictment raised against me, before that was made public I reserved a plane ticket and arrived in The Hague, and then at the airport, Amsterdam airport, I was arrested. So I did not surrender. I took a plane ticket and flew into Amsterdam. All the rest was done by you and the other perpetrators from Holland. I didn't surrender anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
