utterances.text: Having taken the course that you did, do you regard it as appropriate to have a magazine of yours caricaturing things in this way? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like to jeopardise the freedom of the press in Serbia? I like this cartoon very much. I didn't draw it. Unfortunately, I can't draw this well, but it's hilarious and it corresponds to reality. It's hit the nail on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just wanted you to acknowledge it now. When you were asked or required by the Court to stand on their arrival, you agreed to do so, saying that: "Under the threat of the Court that you will sanction my failure to rise by interrupting my testimony in future, I will rise but only before this particular Trial Chamber. Under this threat that you will bring my testimony to an end, I will rise when you enter." Now, the material I have shown you, and it's just a small part, no doubt, of the available total, that shows your real attitude to this Tribunal, doesn't it? Books you publish, things you say --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Robinson threatened to interrupt my testimony, I said before you all that on that threat I shall rise, but the proceedings against me -- in the proceedings against me I will never rise because there is no legal act binding me to do so, and I've already stated that in the proceedings against me I would not take part in satanic rituals, and I abide by that. Now, as far as my relationship and attitude towards this Court is concerned, well, you don't -- obviously don't want to hear my answer, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that you are absolutely determined to use the opportunity afforded you by giving evidence in this Court to give publicity to the answers you've given to this accused's questions, and that means you'll do anything. You'll take the solemn declaration, you'll stand if it's required of you, despite your real attitude being revealed by some of the material we've looked at. Am I not right? You are absolutely determined to use the opportunity afforded you --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not quite right, Mr. Nice. First of all, I took the solemn declaration to tell the truth here, and throughout my testimony I have indeed told the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, everything I knew. Now, that I would use every opportunity to fight politically against this Tribunal, against The Hague Tribunal, against this Court, that is true, too. That is correct. My stand and stance is absolutely negative and I will follow that stance to the end of my life, and you won't be able to make me waiver on that score. And of course everything that you have presented shows that my attitude towards this Court is extremely negative. I question the existence of this Court, the political arguments, legal arguments, and as you can see through the publications of the Serbian National Party, my party [inaudible] this court too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... taken, you're doing two things: You're addressing your political audience back home, and you are the leader of the party with the largest number of votes, I think, there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, all of a sudden you're allowing leading questions. Mr. Nice is not asking me whether I'm using this as a public platform for addressing my political audience. He is simply asserting that, and since you interrupted Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The cross-examiner can ask leading questions. Leading questions are prohibited --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that, Mr. Robinson. I didn't know that. In future I will not object to leading questions. I am testifying here because I was called by Mr. Milosevic as the accused to testify about what I know in favour of his Defence. That's my motive. Everything else are just assumptions by Mr. Nice which cannot be proved. For example, yesterday there was no broadcast. I didn't refuse to testify on that account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear Mr. Nice put another question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's, I'm suggesting to you, your first purpose. And the second purpose relates to the accused, and I'll come to my suggestion to you, broad suggestion covering all your evidence. In the course of the last few days, you have given evidence that would lead to the conclusion that many of the people here awaiting trial, including this accused and yourself, are entirely innocent and shouldn't be here at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many people here have been convicted, although they are innocent, and many are awaiting trial but are completely innocent, and all of these are persons of Serb ethnicity. You have convicted several real criminals. Let me finish my response, because an incomplete response is not a response. I cannot abide by a response that has been interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the same time, you have given evidence against several people who have been here but who are characterised by the fact that they've given evidence adverse to the accused, like Erdemovic, Babic, and even Plavsic. You've given evidence against somebody like -- or adverse to Perisic because, of course, you know that he's written letters in 1998 adverse to the accused. And you've given this evidence both for some and against others without any reference to documentary support, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I mentioned the name of Momcilo Perisic only twice. First, because he was replaced in 1998 on suspicion of having started to work for the Americans' intelligence service, and secondly that volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were under his command in Mostar and he had praised them. This was not a negative comment on my part. It was a positive one. At that time, he was well respected as an able commander. He was replaced, however, pursuant to intelligence information available to the government at the time. I said nothing that is either positive or negative about him, I simply put forward the facts that I know. Furthermore, studying your judgements I came to understand that you very often make use of real criminals, threatening them with high sentences, and then you recruit them, entering into compromises with them, and in return for reducing their sentence -- you're not letting me answer your questions. You're not letting me answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question to you was this: The evidence, favourable and unfavourable, divided between Serbs in the way I've described has been given either wholly or almost wholly without any reference to raw source material, to documents. It's all been on the basis of what you've heard from other people; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. My knowledge was acquired in various ways, sometimes through inspection of documents, sometimes because I was an eyewitness of certain events, sometimes because I was a participant, and sometimes because I heard from relevant sources what actually happened. So the range of my sources is highly complex and cannot be simplified in the way you are doing. However, whenever you don't like my answer, whenever you sense it might be something you don't like, you interrupt me and stop me because you don't really want me to give replies that you don't like. I am saying that you are making use of real criminals. Threatening them with high sentences, you gave them lesser sentences in order to have them appear as witnesses in your favour, and Miroslav Deronjic is an example of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have responded to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move to the next topic, let me just give you this opportunity to help us and yourself. When we come back to the detailed allegations you've made, either for or against individuals, I shall be seeking from you detail of your sources, just as I did with the intelligence material lying behind what you say was the Srebrenica staging. So I'm giving you notice now. I shall want details of the people to whom you spoke and your sources on which you relied for the generalised evidence which is the Defence case that you've advanced. Do you understand me? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand everything, Mr. Nice, much better than you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to some of the various things that you've said in the course of these conflicts. You've made the point that you're a very much published man, and you have sought to say that from time to time you said things that were untrue for a particular purpose. Can you now, please, explain in a little more detail for what period of time and for what purpose did you say things that were untrue?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I didn't say it like that. What I said - and I recall it very well - was the following: Setting out untrue things if the entire public knows that they are not true but are simply amusing and said for a certain particular purpose, this is neither lying nor setting out untruths. This is witticisms, sarcasm, and so on. I was waging a political propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic from the Vance-Owen Plan until the beginning of 1998. In this propaganda war, various insults were bandied about on both sides, serious accusations. It wasn't Mr. Milosevic personally who did that but his party certainly did. The secret police was working on destroying the Serb Radical Party. The defence mechanism of our party, not simply mine but of all my colleagues, was to use means of propaganda, those that your masters in the West use to a large extent, beginning with false accusations that Saddam Hussein has weapons of mass destruction in order to justify aggression, only to have it later transpire that he didn't have such weapons at all. It was your masters in the West who taught me how to wage a propaganda war, but I have not yet risen to their level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the time scale for your untruths was 1993, would that be, to 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time frame in which the Serb Radical Party waged a propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic, his party, and their government was from mid-1993 to early 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the focus of the propaganda was the accused Milosevic himself, was it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He and his party, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, having said things and had things printed that were untrue, have you gone around the process of correcting them ever? Have you published work saying, well, it's time everybody knew that what I was saying was untrue and time I set the record straight, or are you still publishing the books that contain the same propaganda and untruths, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all -- first of all, I never renounced any of my public statements, but in 1998, for example, and in later years, in 2000 and after the fall of Mr. Milosevic from power, frequently in the interviews I gave to various television and radio stations and newspapers, explained that that was when I was waging a propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic and that those statements were made within the scope of that war. Even the former Minister of Justice, Vladan Batic, did what you're doing now. He collected excerpts from my previous speeches against Mr. Milosevic and his wife and started quoting them from the rostrum after the coup d'etat. After him, I took the floor and explained these previous attacks in the same way, but when Mr. Milosevic was powerful and when he was in power, Vladan Batic was hiding in a mouse hole, and it was I who had the courage, when Mr. Milosevic had the support of the West after the Dayton agreement, to wage a very difficult political fight against him and his policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. When we look at the material, reflect the things that you've said, we've got your explanation in mind. Is there anybody else individually about whom you said things that were untrue? Think back.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again: I wasn't telling untruths but waging a propaganda war, carrying out my professional political duty. Speaking untruths is something quite different. If you want to say that the American President George Bush was lying when he said that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, then you can say that I was lying when I was attacking Mr. Milosevic. As long as you don't dare say that George Bush was lying or telling untruths, you cannot accuse me of that. You have to have the same criterion towards everyone who acts in this way when performing a political office. Tell me that Bush was lying and then I will admit that I was lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I invite you, please, to speak more quietly. You're capable of doing it and it's very difficult to focus on your answers when you speak at the volume you do. You claim to be the leader of a democratic party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the president. I never termed myself a leader. I'm the president of the Serb Radical Party which has a democratic character.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You believe in democracy and the power of the people to make decisions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I sincerely believe in democracy and in the right of the people to make decisions concerning their own fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As an educated man, do you believe that you owe a duty to use your education, knowledge responsibly, including responsibly towards your fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always used my knowledge in a responsible manner, even in this confrontation with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How does that, then, square with your willingness to tell by way of propaganda things that are blatantly false?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When some things are evidently untrue the person pronouncing them cannot be described as a liar. In political life there is something called a political tit for tat. In the heated atmosphere of political life, this is an exchange of blows. Sometimes the blows are below the belt. I did not refrain from such blows either, but only if the opposite side acted towards me in that way first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question by way of introduction to the quotations I'm going to put to you is this: Nenad Canak is a politician you know well?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad Canak -- you don't want to hear my response about Nenad Canak? Nenad Canak is one of the most immoral people in Serbia. He cannot even be described as a politician because his party can never cross the threshold at elections, but he's a mercenary of Western intelligence agencies, paid to implement an anti-Serb subversive policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In a statement to investigators of this Tribunal, which I'm going to lay on the overhead projector and is available to the Chamber and accused if it's wanted, I just want to put one thing about your attitude.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who made this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nenad Canak. Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that I made a statement to The Hague investigators. I have never made any statement to The Hague investigators. When I arrived on the -- in The Hague, I'm started insisting on it but your colleagues have been avoiding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see the statement. What about it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, put it at the -- have you got it there, Mr. Nort? Paragraph 46, top of the page. Top of the page. Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't speak English. I don't understand what is being shown to me in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters will translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just read you this short paragraph which concludes with an observation of yours towards your own people. "Seselj became popular and powerful because he got in touch with money."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "He never joined coalitions, which is a very important strategy for a fascist party. Seselj had to be the 'Messiah' so people would follow him. Seselj is a populist and a liar and always has answers. He is convinced and he convinces people with his arguments." Then this: "On one occasion Vuk Draskovic and Seselj were talking and Draskovic asked Seselj: How can you lie so much? Seselj replied: In Serbia I have one million illiterate people so I do not have to worry about my political future." That last sentence that is attributed to you, is that your attitude to gaining and retaining support, that you can say what you like to people who may be less literate than you or illiterate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad Canak and Vuk Draskovic are both liars, traitors of the Serbian people, and agents of Western Intelligence services. That is my attitude towards all their statements. I never published anything like this, that in Serbia I have one million illiterate people so I don't have to worry about my political future. That is their lie, their fabrication. There is a problem, because you in the OTP take for granted everything said by Serbian traitors, and then you base your false indictments on their statements, the statements of people like Vuk Draskovic and Nenad Canak. When I asked to have disclosed to me the material by the OTP about Draskovic's Serbian Guard, they refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... move on. Can we look, please, at number 8, Der Spiegel, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it from that answer you deny saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do deny it. You cannot find it in any statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer wasn't clear because you said you'd never published anything like that, but I think the reference was to something said orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I just want to be sure; you're denying saying it orally as well, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I deny that I ever said anything like this, and I assert that both Nenad Canak and Vuk Draskovic are absolute liars and foreign agents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've explained before, Mr. Seselj, that I find it helpful if you just answer the question, and if you don't answer the particular question that's put it sometimes can create confusion, certainly in my mind. Now, I may not have the necessary intellectual capacity to deal with your answers in the way you give them, so perhaps you could help me by simply answering the question that's asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, my answers are quite simple, but I want them to be complete, because a trial of this kind cannot be a quiz where one has to give a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document that's being distributed comes in various parts. I think it will probably be necessary for me to guide the usher through its display, if I can have it back. The first one, this comes from Der Spiegel, and I think it's Der Spiegel in 1991, so it's before the period of any campaign against this accused. As you say in this, the passage you're looking at at the moment: "What would you do if you were President of Serbia? "I would mobilise all Serbs, amputate Croatia in a quick war, and then inform the international community about the new Serbian borders. "What borders would that be? "Aside from the provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, republics Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia and Montenegro should be attached to Serbia, as well as the territories in Croatia which are inhabited by Serbs, with the border along the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line." Now, that was your position then. That's the position of your party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the standpoint of the Serb Radical Party spoken before the war as early as July, before the army began military operations at all, and of course had I been in government, but unfortunately I was not, I would have amputated Croatia and prevented any kind of war. Unfortunately, we had a government that was not up to that, and that made it possible for the Western powers to intervene and for us to lose the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This identifies -- and we're going to come to Greater Serbia in more detail probably tomorrow, but this identifies, doesn't it, the platform of your party and its reliance upon the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line, which is also slightly more defined in your testimony as actually being the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica. That is the western ethnic border, Serbian border, which should become the state border of Serbia border, and will certainly one day become that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in -- picking up something that His Honour Judge Bonomy was concerned about, and again to which we may return if time permits later, is the choice of that line language connected or language related?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is linked to the nation and language. The difference between Serbs and Croats is a linguistic one. All Shtokavians are Serbs regardless of whether they are Orthodox, Catholics, or Muslims. All Chakavians are Croats. The Kajkavians in Croatia used to be Slovenians but they were transformed into Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're speaking with knowledge that may not be available because we haven't touched on it in detail with this Chamber. In the area of the former Yugoslavia with which we're concerned, there is a dialect system, a system of different dialects, and it may be broken down into three: The Shtokavian dialect; the Chakavian dialect, which is typically spoken west, in Istria and possibly down the Littoral; and the Kajkavian dialect, which is spoken to the north, in the area of Zagreb and thereabouts. And it's those dialects and separating those dialects out that lies behind your assertion that everybody apart from the speakers of those two other dialects is a Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. One of the greatest Serbian linguists of all times, a Catholic from Dubrovnik, Milan Resetar, in the late 19th century and early 20th century proved in a scholarly manner that Shtokavian, Chakavian, and -- Chakavian, Kajkavian, and Shtokavian are three different languages. As regards various dialects within Serbian, there is the old Shtokavian spoken in Macedonia, central Shtokavian in Prizren, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause. We will go into this if it's relevant and if we have time, but you must recognise that if you're going to let out expert knowledge of the kind you're revealing at this speed, it's going to be difficult to conceal. I just wanted to establish at this early stage that this chosen line is indeed dialect connected and we'll come back to it later. Can we look now at the next document --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To conceal or to understand? That line is based on languages approximately. Chakavian, the Chakavian language is almost extinct. Kajkavian is still spoken in the three counties that were in the Croatian Banovina before the break-up of Austria. That is the Zagreb, Krizevac, and Varazdin counties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, the Chamber, if it finds the topic interesting, and although the book could only at best be used as a guide, because it may of course bear national partisan reflections in its maps, I don't know, but at 68 of Exhibit 336 you can find some initial guidance. The book is in as a map, it's not in as anything else, but you may find some guidance and it may be that later on if I need a map, I'll look at that as a possible examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's look now at something else, a document from 6th of December, 1990, which was reprinted in your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice is repeating his usual practice. It wasn't Mr. Seselj that started speaking about the Chakavian, Kajkavian, and Shtokavian dialects. It was Mr. Nice who mentioned the dialects when presenting certain assertions, obviously not knowing what he was talking about, and then he did not allow the witness to answer the question that he had put. He was the one who put these expert linguistic questions, not Mr. Seselj, and then he doesn't allow Mr. Seselj to give expert answers to these questions. He should be careful about the questions he puts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. The witness has confirmed at this early stage, because I know the matter was troubling -- not troubling, of interest to, one of the members of the Bench, and indeed the line is linguistically related and we've got the broadest outlines at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this next document. This is an interview with you on the 6th of December, 1990, and this is what you then said: "Regarding Croatia, we the Serb Chetniks, are constantly telling the new Ustasha leader, Franjo Tudjman, and the new Ustasha authorities in Croatia, not to play games with the Serbian people living in the areas of the present improvised Croatian state community. That is the Serb territory, populated by Serbian people, and we shall never allow it to be separated from its mother country." First of all, you can see the quote on the Serbian version. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said and that's what I repeat today. Perhaps we won't manage to get these ethnic Serb boundaries along the Karlovac-Karlobag-Virovitica line that quickly, however the Serb Radical Party and the Serb nation as a whole will never give up on liberating the Republic of the Serb Krajina from the Croatian occupation, and that remains the vow of all honourable Serbs. This occupation of the Serb Krajina has to stop some day. We will insist on peaceful means. However, even if it turns to be necessary to take the other road, we won't evade that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at what you said in 1990, and this is an example of what was being publicised, which is why I'm interested in it. What was, in 1990, a Ustasha? Was it every Croat who didn't agree to be counted as a Serb? Was it only those who actively supported Tudjman's party? What was a Ustasha, a word you use so regularly?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: An Ustasha is a Croat clero-fascist. In their past, the Croats had a very strong fascist movement of a clerical nature, and that was the Ustasha movement that committed a genocide against the Serb people during the Second World War, and that Ustasha movement was in recent times renewed by Franjo Tudjman. Ustashas are Croatian clero-fascists because it had a stronghold in the Catholic church and high-ranking Catholic clergymen personally took part in the slaughter of the Serb people. Filipovic Majstorovic was one of those from Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See if you can help us, please. If there was --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to explain. I mean, I'm answering your questions what the word Ustasha means in my terminology and in the terminology of the Serb Radical Party. Well, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice has another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you were to have encountered, at the time you made this interview, a person in the part of what is now called Croatia but lying east of the Karlobag line and between there and the Bosnian boundary, and if this was a person who simply chose to describe himself or thought of himself as a Croat, would he be a Ustasha simply for that reason?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is what I want to know: Put yourself into -- so we know who you're referring to when you use this phrase. We go to such a village or such a town. Who in that town are to understand themselves as addressed by you when you use the word "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who expose themselves from the positions of an Ustasha ideology. Those who accept the Ustasha ideology are Ustashas. Ustasha is an ideological term, like a Nazi in Germany, like a fascist in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, for example, when we come, as we will, to Vukovar and to the residents there, did what happened to the residents there depend on whether they were identified as Ustashas or not; and if so, how did the Ustashas come to be identified? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Ustashas in Vukovar, and during the war Ustashas killed Serb civilians in Vukovar. However, that does not mean that all Croats in Vukovar were Ustashas, and I never said any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While this document is being handed round, you spoke yourself, when referring to your studies, effectively of the power, and you've spoken generally of the power of propaganda. Do you understand the significance in the development of crimes in the course of war -- do you understand the significance of propaganda in the development of crimes in the course of war?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda that is of a criminal nature is explicit in that, and I never engaged in the propaganda of crimes. Never, ever. You cannot say that my ideology of a Greater Serbia causes criminality in its own right. That is an untenable thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you understand -- do you understand the significance of labelling the enemy or the opposition in a way that will make them the object of dislike, hatred, and ultimately of dehumanisation? Do you understand that process?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, again you are putting things the wrong way. What does that mean, to turn someone into an object of hatred? First of all, those who were in the Croatian government in Tudjman's regime who made the Serbs the object of hatred did that through their own anti-Serb steps and their open renewal of an Ustasha ideology. I was a vocal critic of that kind of policy, and I did so in public. Because if Franjo Tudjman himself said several times that the Independent State of Croatia from the Second World War was an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people, then he declared himself an Ustasha. I wasn't the one who declared himself a Ustasha. After that kind of a statement, I persistently attacked them as Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You haven't actually answered the question, which was a matter of principle and arguably of great importance to this case, but in light of your answer I'll ask you a second question of general propaganda principle and then return to the first question. Are you aware, in the use or abuse of propaganda in war, of the value of attributing to your enemy your own wicked intentions so that you say the other side is about to kill us, all in order to stimulate your side to go and kill them? Are you aware of the significance of that as a rudimentary tool of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are partial and therefore you are imputing things. You are trying rid the Croats of their guilt, and you're trying to ascribe that guilt to the Serbs. Everything that happened in this war and before this war was regularly initiated by the Croat side, and every move made by the Serbs was only a reaction to what the Croats had already done. You are trying to put things the other way around. That's the problem. And you cannot lead me that way through your logical frame of mind because I'm not a sheep to be shepherded that way. I'm trying to answer all your questions fully but you keep interrupting me because you're not happy with my answers. You want me to confirm what you've been saying through my own answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two parts of the general topic of propaganda that I might like to put to this witness but now this next question before we look at the next clip -- or the first video clip: In the course of your up and down relationship with this accused over the years, did he ever seek to restrain you in your use of the terminology that you used?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "restrain"? Am I a horse and is he supposed to rein me in? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the question is easy enough to understand. Did he say, write, or do anything to you to stop you saying, writing the sorts of things that you did?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrested me a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the purpose of stopping you saying the particular things you did about other ethnic groups, or was it for other purposes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to remove me from political life for at least a certain period of time. However, every one of those arrests was invariably supported by the pro-Western parties in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at a bit of video, please, if we can. I think it comes from the 21st of April, 1991, in Jagodnjak. I'm sorry, it's on Sanction, is it? It's on Sanction I should tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember that speech or speeches along that line that you were making?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I admire myself for having put things so wisely 15 years ago. I still stand by that. And had I been in power, they could not have seceded at all. They could not have taken anything that was Serbian. They could have only taken the Zagreb, Krizevac, and Varazdin counties. Nothing else. Regrettably, I was not in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whatever the state of the history and its bearing on this case, by the time you were making statements like this, the Republic of Croatia within the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia had existed as an identifiable unit for many years, hadn't it? You may not like that fact, but it had existed as a unit like that for many years.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer? Well, you didn't put it in the form of a question. There was a Croatian federal unit from the end of the war until 1991. However, that federal unit that was called Croatia was a federal unit of the Croat people and the Serbs living in Croatia, and according to all the constitutional text up to Tudjman's time, the Serbs were constituent people within it, which meant that its constitutional status could not be changed without the agreement of the Serbs. I cautioned about that before the war, too, before the skirmishes in Borovo Selo. This was April, 1991. I cautioned that Croatia cannot secede and not take away with it what is Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question derived from the first -- the previous question is this: Making statements like this in respect of the territory of an identifiable unit of the kind I've described and you've just dealt with is to invite war and bloodshed, isn't it, because the only way you're going to change so dramatically the shape of a unit that others regard as appropriate for them and a reflection of their nationality, the only way you're going to change boundaries like that is by war; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're absolutely wrong, and again you're twisting the truth. Tudjman and his authorities were showing with increasing openness their intention to secede from Yugoslavia. My response was an answer to their intentions and their statements: You cannot secede. You cannot take Croatia away within its current boundaries. If you're seceding, you can only take that part of the territory which is undeniably Croat. According to the Yugoslav legal system, the -- there was never a right of federal units to secede. That was prohibited by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think -- I understand entirely what you're saying here, but again if I may say, it doesn't really address the question. No one's suggesting -- at least, I don't think Mr. Nice is suggesting that it's not perfectly reasonable to respond to Croatian ambition by asserting your own view that that is unconstitutional, illegal, ought not to happen, should be resisted, it's the tone that the question is about, not about the idea behind it, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My tone, Mr. Bonomy, matches my temperament, and I am not going to adjust to anyone from that point of view. My words were precise, clear, focused and aimed in a very particular direction: If you want to secede, you cannot do so without a war. And it was clear to everyone. Slovenia could secede without a war. I attacked the JNA for intervening in Slovenia at all because there were no territories in dispute. However, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina could not have taken place -- could not have seceded without a war, but Macedonia could have seceded without a war. But Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia could not have seceded without a war and those who were working on this secession actually knew that it could not take place without a war and they were preparing for a war. A few months before that, the military intelligence showed the illegal arming of Croatian paramilitaries before the war, in January 1991. So it was quite clear what the Croat authorities were preparing, and the response had to be a very definite one. My response was the response of an opposition politician from Serbia, not the government. And at that time, that opposition party was not even in parliament. At that time in April 1991, we were not even in parliament. It was only in June that year that we won our first seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, you do respond with a constructive argument in support of the position you adopt, but you have to bear in mind, and I suspect it's the same in Serbia as it is certainly in Western European countries, that people often only hear or read the headlines, the particularly prominent parts of anything that's said, and it's the tone in which certain things are said that might cause concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's -- I think it's a convenient time. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've been asked about or prompted to deal with exhibits. The matters I've about putting to the witness at the moment, which are to do with things he said or things he has accepted saying and has given his explanation for what he said in answer to questions, and it doesn't seem to me necessary to produce a document because it's all on the transcript. I'm, of course, happy to produce them as documents if anybody wants me to. The video is different, because, of course, it shows the manner and so I'd ask that certainly for the video of the witness to be produced, and the position will change when we move to another area of things that this witness said which bear more on the facts of the indictment. When looking at things, I'm quite happy for them not to be produced and perhaps Ms. Dicklich and I and the Registry can discuss matters, either at the end of the day, and see if we can agree to them very quickly as a proposition for putting forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at the next document, which is slightly out of order, I think. No, it's not. Yes, it is. It's the 6th of December, 1990, number 14.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the tab number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry if I haven't been giving the tab numbers. It's tab 13. My apologies. I forgot that you've got them in tabbed binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you'll go, please, to the marked page, Mr. Seselj. This is a statement of yours on the 6th of December, 1990, in your magazine with your picture on the front of it. And the highlighted passage, which the Chamber can find on page 9 of 23 - and it's on page 11 of the Serbian - on page 9 -- halfway down page 9 of -- less than halfway down: "Thus the Croatian people should not fear Serbian retaliation of that kind, of that nature, however, Croats must be punished. They should be punished in a manner in which nations and states are being punished in a civilised world for crimes committed by their regimes during wars, that being the loss of territories." You see, your rhetoric at the time - this is in 1990 - was in terms of the Croats losing territory. What do you say to that? Why should you say such things?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should first like to remind you of a statement made by the great French Cardinal Richelieu who said, "Just give me one sentence from any text and I will find enough arguments to sentence the author to death." You have singled out a single sentence only from this entire paragraph, but the answer is contained in the previous part of the paragraph. What I say is not all Germans -- I mean, this has to do with the Croat crimes in the Second World War. And then the presenter of the show on television -- this is when I appeared as a candidate for president in the campaign of 1990, and the presenter is asking me: "It's not the fault of the entire Serb people, is it?" And I say: "Well, you know, not all Germans were in favour of Hitler and the Nazis. There were Germans who perished in Hitler's camps, who were killed and who had to flee abroad. But they were a small minority. It was the German people who were punished for Hitler's crimes in the Second World War although all Germans were not Nazis. How were the German people punished? Most Germans were in favour of the Nazi regime and the Germans were duly punished because they lost a great portion of their territories, eastern Prussia --" and then there is a mistake here, it says Sweden, but it's not Sweden -- "and then it was divided according to the will of the allies into three smaller states; East Germany, West Germany, and Austria. Almost half a century had to go by before Germany was reunified, and it is a question when its third constituent part, Austria, will be able to reunite with the German entity. Germans also had to pay certain reparations. They were under the tutorship of the great powers."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We give you the whole article, of course --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not letting me answer. Please, I'm just asking for one paragraph and you want only one sentence from a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, exceptionally, I'm going to allow a long answer because what you're putting is consistent with your theory, the Prosecution theory, it's a very serious matter, that you have evidence of this witness speaking of the loss of territories at the expense of Croatia, so let him provide the explanation. Go ahead, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text reads as follows: "Germans were under the tutorship of the great powers, but as opposed to the German case, although the Croats in terms of proportions, in terms of population numbers committed much greater crimes. This improvised Croatian state was seemingly rewarded for this. They got territories that were never Croatian territories in history. For example, Dubrovnik, which was traditionally a Serbian city and where Serb Catholics lived for centuries. We believe that this question of the responsibility of the Croat people should be brought up again. Of course, we have no intention to retaliate against the Croats in an 'eye-for-an-eye' manner, to remove one Croatian head for every Serbian head. No. We, the Serbs, are traditionally a chivalrous people and the hands of our people were never stained with the blood of innocent civilians, women, children and the elderly. We, the Serbs, are fighters on the battlefield, and once we defeat our enemy in the battlefield, we do not keep on tormenting or harassing him. We have a chivalrous attitude towards the enemy himself as well. Therefore, the Croatian people should not fear Serbian retaliation of that kind, of that nature. We shall not do that. We shall remain a chivalrous, dignified people in the future as well, however, the Croats must be punished. They should be punished in a manner in which nations and states are being punished in the civilised world for crimes committed by their regimes during wars. That is to say, by the loss of territories." That is my position in comprehensive terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us in summary form now the explanation of all of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a historical topic that I am debating here. Croatia was rewarded after the Second World War. It got many Italian territories; all of Istria, Zadar, and the coast. They expelled 300.000 Italians from there instead of bearing certain consequences for the Ustasha crimes. The Croat Ustashas killed a million Serbs. No reparations were ever paid. Crimes were concealed, covered up. And this is in 1992, so it's outside any war context. This is my position with regard to that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are -- there are two matters in there, though. One is that the Croatian state were, you say, unjustly rewarded by being given additional territory after the war, but that's not what you're saying in the part that's identified. The part that's been picked up in the question is that the Croats must be punished in a manner you say in which nations and states are being punished in a civilised world for crimes. I don't follow that argument at all about what happened to Germany. You present it as if it was all planned that it would be divided into two or three parts and so on. As you know, that was the result of historical developments. But you're talking about them being punished by losing territories. Now, does that mean that you -- you were urging the government to try to seize territory from Croatia, or the people to seize territory from Croatia? What had you in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'm not appealing to the government here at all. I'm just presenting my own personal views and position. If Germany was punished -- and what you say is not true; the allies did plan the division of Germany before the war ended and the division was established by plan, of Berlin into three parts and Germany into three parts. The allies prepared and planned for that before the war was over, three occupying zones. Germany lost a vast amount of territory. It lost Eastern Silezia, Eastern Prussia, and it had to pay war reparations. Not all, but it paid quite a lot. Whereas the Serbs that suffered at the hands of the Ustashas, no reparation was ever paid and the Croats were rewarded by being given far more territory than they were entitled to ethnically speaking. It is my position that they should have been punished by a loss of territory, and I think that it was a great injustice, the establishment of a Croatian federal unit, but that's my own personal position. What's that got to do with Mr. Milosevic at all? I stepped out of Milosevic's prison and appeared on television. Two or three days before that, before I appeared on television, I was in prison where this view was presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This statement is made, what, 48 years after the events that it relates to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Forty-eight years? So -- so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a thousand -- I would say the same thing a thousand years after the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was it you had in mind when -- if you had been in power at the time you made this statement, what was it you would have had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. First of all, at the time I made the statement, my party was outside the law. The authorities of Mr. Milosevic refused to register my party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you had been in power -- if you had been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can't take it that simply, the way you would like, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am responding in like kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- can answer the question but I cannot have you suggesting the answer to me. Tudjman was already well in power in Croatia. He came to power in the month of May of that year, six months previously. So that is a response to what had already happened in Croatia beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So my question, my simple question to you is: If you had been in power in Serbia at that time, what would you have proposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this isn't a question of power in Serbia. Here you would have to be in power in Yugoslavia. You would have to have been in power in Yugoslavia because that year I published in Pogledi, a paper from Kragujevac, my vision of the restructuring of Yugoslavia, and I called for the abolishment of all federal units and the division of Yugoslavia into 30 districts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it may be my mistake, but I understood that this was said when you were a presidential candidate. Was that for the presidency of Yugoslavia? I thought it was Serbia, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I was a candidate for the presidency of Serbia but I'm presenting the political stances with respect to the developments in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's the context in which I ask you the question. If you had been in power as a result of success, what would you have done to follow up this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As president of the Republic of Serbia, I could have done nothing from that position. However, I'm presenting my positions on a specific concrete issue, topic, whereas you want to suggest to me that everything I say in a lengthy programme is just my presidential programme, electoral programme. I stress at the beginning of the interview that I am presenting the programme of my party comprehensively, in its entirety, not only linked to the presidential functions, because pursuant to the constitution, the powers of the president of the republic are so small that of himself he cannot do anything. Mr. Milosevic, on the basis of his position as president of the Republic, had practically no power at all. He had enormous political influence on the basis of the fact that his party was the largest party in parliament and had formed a government. Take a look at the constitution of Serbia and you will see that there are no authorisations with that function in that post. You can do nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice. I didn't mean to take over that part of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- exhibited in full because the witness wishes the context to be given. But I'm not going to ask him any more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at now, please, something that you said on the 18th of July, 1991. For the interpreters, it's tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon suggests that we just deal with the exhibits now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, can this one -- I'd better go back there and review which ones I should have asked to be exhibited. I think it's probably only the video, which was the video of the 21st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 873.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then if this one could become the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, interview to the -- that was just referred to will be Exhibit 874.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm obliged. And if we could now look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the entire interview or just the part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The entire interview, and in light of the challenge to context, I fear that it's probably better to put it in in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can look, then, please, at tab 12 for the interpreters, interview on the 18th of July, 1991. So we're back into 1991. And if you'd be good enough, Mr. Seselj, to go to the place I hope marked as page 5 of the Serbian text. It's page 4 of the English text. Before we look at the passage concerned, the enthusiasm with which Slovenia was let go reflected the fact, of course, that Slovenia was a convenient single language, single ethnic potential state; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Slovenes were a separate nation. They had a language of their own and lived on their own ethnic compact territory with very few exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But Serbs, of course, lived on all the other territories, depending on how they're defined, but in any event they lived on all the other territories. And so we see this quotation of yours. It's at the bottom of page 4: "It might not be a definitive power, but as far as you Slovenes are concerned, it does represent a very, very serious insurmountable force, you know. You see, while the Serbs are well-disposed towards you, you can walk. Afterwards, you will not be able to. Later on, we are going to turn Yugoslavia into Serboslavia, and then you can forget about secession." Now, by all means, if you think that this needs interpreting by reference to other questions and answers in the context, take us to those, but what I'd like your help with is this: How do you think the promise of creating out of most or all, even, of the former Yugoslavia Serboslavia is going to be taken by your listeners or readers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My listeners and readers were Slovenes. This is an interview to the Slovenian television, and as a part to all the officials of Serbia and Yugoslavia, I supported Slovenian separatism. And at one point in time it seems that the Slovenes were wearing -- wondering whether to secede or not. I supported them. I went along their lines and even dared them to do so. And an answer to the question can be found in a very short previous paragraph: "Croatia cannot secede so easily, at least not as easily as Slovenia." And the Slovenes made their biggest mistake -- well, you keep avoiding my answer, hearing my answer. The answer is contained in a previous text, a very brief paragraph, just six lines long. Why are you so impatient? You want to have short experts to build up your own visions, Mr. Nice. Well, that cannot be done. It is an integral text and I would just like to refer you to a brief paragraph that went before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, may I be -- or with Mr. Robinson's permission, may I be allowed to read the previous paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him -- where is the paragraph you want to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Middle of the page in the English, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's around the middle of the page. Just six lines, where I say this: "It is not that easy for Croatia to secede, anyway not as easy as it would be for Slovenia. The Slovenians made their biggest mistake when they allowed themselves to become an instrument in Croatian hands. The Croats are constantly holding the Slovenes back by comparing themselves to Slovenia, by making it seem identical to the one in Slovenia. It is not the same situation at all because what is holding Croatia back is not the same thing that is holding Slovenia back. You have every chance of seceding. The Croats do not. At least, not within the present borders." Now, why am I saying all this? I am saying all this because the Croats are sending the JNA to Slovenia, Stipe Mesic and Ante Markovic, because the Croats are preventing Slovenian secession. They wish to link up the Croatian issue and the Slovenian issue in one package so that they can promulgate it more easily. I am telling the Slovenes to secede and not to link themselves up with the Croatians. I said you Slovenes are free to leave straight away, you can leave straight away. Croatia can't because they have a large percentage of Serbs living on its territory. So that is the essence of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you would have to look at the whole interview, because throughout the interview I support the Slovenians in their wish to secede.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I have to say frankly I don't understand how that explains this statement "Later on we are going to turn Yugoslavia into Serboslavia." You have attempted to put it in context but I have to say frankly that I still don't understand the connection between the paragraph to which you referred and the statement about turning Yugoslavia into Serboslavia, which was Mr. Nice's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am letting the Slovenes know: Listen, you are a compact territory, you can secede, you have the right to secede, it's in your interest to secede, go ahead, go, but don't spend too much time thinking about it and link yourselves up to Croatia because that will bring problems. And in all the other territories you have Serb inhabitants. Once the Slovenes leave, Yugoslavia to all intents and purposes is Serboslavia because the Serbs are the majority nation in what is left of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there were almost half as many Serbs there. There might have been two and a half or three million Slovenes, I don't know exactly how much, but with the departure of the Slovenes, all that remains is territories inhabited by Serbs in greater or lesser concentration but you have them everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this is the point of my question: If you were a person pretending to be, as you would have it, a Croatian, or pretending to be or mistakenly thinking himself to be a Bosnian listening to this interview and you say you're going to create a Serboslavia, do you think it reasonable that they might fear something in the form of a Serb takeover of the territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm a democrat and I count on free democratic elections. I rely on them. In the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, where the Serbs were the majority nation, the Serbs divided into a number of parties and the rest formed one party for the most part. So why would I instil fear in others? I am inciting the Slovenes in leave, encouraging them to leave, and here my position is quite clear; that Croatia has no chance of seceding. So I thought that if Slovenia were to secede quickly, then Croatia would not be able to secede at all after that. So that's the point of this. If Croatia and Slovenia and in one block, form one bloc, then they become a terrible problem, whereas if Slovenia leaves of its own, then there are no -- there is no more chance for Croatia to secede as -- at all and then it would have to look for a compromise within what is left of Yugoslavia. That's the point of it and that's the logic of all that, and that's quite clear to one and all, and that's what I state in that previous paper. The Croatians have no chance of seceding. I say that expressly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I stand all of that. I understand what you claim to have been saying, but you still haven't answered the question that was asked of you. Don't you think that would put fear into the other peoples who would remain within Yugoslavia because of the way in which and the tone in which you were presenting this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the Serbs are not vampire -- a vampire nature or scarecrows or anybody there to instil fear. Why would the Serbs instil fear? What negative experiences which -- are there which people -- would lead people to be afraid of the Serbs? Why fear? I think it is wonderful to be a member of the Serb nation but it is far from me to force anybody to be a Serb if they don't want to. But I'm talking about -- I want to tell the people who split from the Serb nation a long time ago, generations ago, that they have the same roots and that they are part of the Serb same nation. I've been trying to do that for the past 20 years, and I leave my texts to live beyond me, beyond the grave, as testimony to that, and I hope that one day they will see the light of day and people will see the light by reading them, because those who step down from the Serb people by becoming Catholics or Muslims were always used by Serb enemies against the Serb people. So how much longer are we going to stand for that? And it's happening today too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this one had better go in as a whole again because he's wanting to refer back to the context. So may this be exhibited. I think it better be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I insist upon all my texts being introduced into evidence in their entirety because they can only be viewed objectively in their entirety, comprehensively. I don't -- I don't ask that any of them be admitted, but if they are admitted, then they should be admitted in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will leave that decision on a case-by-case basis, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that interview of 18 June 1991 will be Exhibit 875.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before I miss the point and before we move to the next document, that interview, of course, in May of 1991 was after declarations of independence by both Slovenia and Croatia, wasn't it? You were declaring an intention to create a Serboslavia. 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not before Slovenia's independence. The Slovenians showed their intent and then the army intervened, then they were in two minds. So my interview comes when they were debating in two minds and that is why I'm so suggestive and saying go, go, go, unless you go now you'll never leave, you'll never be able to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at the next document, and for the benefit of the booths, this covers tabs 15, 21 and 22. There may be a lack of chronology but I don't think it will harm. It's from a book of the witness called Politics as a Conscientious Challenge, and if we look at them in the order in which they appear in the book. First one you will find on English page 3 of 13 it's recorded, but you haven't got all 13 pages. 3 of 13. Here's part of an interview at a press conference of yours, and this is what you were --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that before me. I have some other text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Bring it back. Ms. Dicklich will find the -- we've given you the right text.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't provide me with the press conference text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a question which says -- I said press conference, it's probably wrong. There is an question from ON: "Has it already come to it, as you stated in yesterday's press conference, 'If executions --'"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a press conference, it's an interview for the paper ON.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "If executions of bare-handed Serbs begin taking place, the only remaining option is an eye-for-an-eye action." Did you in the previous -- do you remember a press conference saying something about eye for eye actions if executions of bare-handed Serbs took place?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview was published on the 24th of May, 1991, and here there was a threat of caution. There was a press conference and parts of it were probably published in the press and they can be found. Here we have a question with respect to the contents of that press conference and I provide a very concrete answer that you have highlighted. You want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why don't you read it, yes. We'll follow it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is this: "Yes it has! We have already deployed several Chetnik groups in Zagreb and other towns across Croatia, which are trained in sabotage and terrorist activities. And if the Serb civilians start to be massacred, the Chetniks will strike at Zagreb and other concentrations of Croats, using their full strength. You know, when one retaliates, revenge is blind. There would be innocent victims, too, but what can you do. Let the Croats think about that first. We shall not strike first, but if they should strike, we're not going to pay attention to where our blows land. Also, unless the army disarms the Ustashas immediately, there will be a lot of blood." Now, we didn't have these groups. I threatened, don't massacre Serb civilians, that's what I'm saying, because if you massacre Serb civilians, we'll have to take our revenge and revenge is blind, and the rest is quite clear. So I'm issuing a caution, I am warning them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, lower your volume. You're shouting now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you had -- is it right factually that you had deployed Chetnik groups in Zagreb and across Croatia and that they were there to retaliate by way of revenge if you deemed it appropriate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a bluff. I've just been telling you that. I am threatening in the face of a concrete danger. I'm saying to them don't you dare do that because then terrible things will come to pass. So I'm cautioning them, warning him. The threat is a strong one, perhaps too strong, but I'm saying don't you dare do anything of the kind. And this was a bluff, of course, because we didn't have those Chetnik groups to deploy anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See what you said on page 6 of 13 in the English. And it's in the next extract you've got in your book, I think. The magazine asks you under the cross-heading "Youths Will Take Away the Seal of Shame," "What about Bosnia, let alone the others?" And you said this: "Bosnia is undoubtedly Serbian, and if any Muslim fundamentalists do not like that, they will have to pack their suitcases and leave." And you were asked: "But the majority of its population is Muslim." To which you responded: "So what! If they become loyal citizens of Serbia, they will enjoy full citizens' rights and human freedoms. If not, they will have to start packing!" Let me remind you, when we look at the Kosovo section of the evidence, you were able to justify proposals that people should move out on the grounds that they had comparatively recently populated Kosovo from Albania. What are you doing here, suggesting to Muslim fundamentalists that they would have to pack their suitcases and leave, expelling your own people?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm suggesting -- no. Suggesting, no. Just the fundamentalists. And you know what great danger the fundamentalists are to the world --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How are you --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and all over the world, especially Muslim fundamentalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pack their bags and leave, Mr. Seselj, and how is the person listening to this --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, every person listening to this interview or reading it in the papers knows whether they are a fundamentalist or not as far as they themselves are concerned, and I draw your attention that far before this the Islamic declaration was published by Alija Izetbegovic in which he expressly claims that it is impossible to have a life together between Muslims and Christians. So that is that concrete danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, once again I ask you to lower the volume. Do not shout.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that mean that Mr. Izetbegovic should have packed his bags and left? Is that what you're saying? And, if so, where was it you were going to exile him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, Mr. Nice, are reasoning in the way a small child would. This is a general threat to the fundamentalists, exclusively to fundamentalists and aimed at fundamentalists. It does not bring into question the right of Muslims as citizens of a future state if Yugoslavia really were to be broken down as was talked about previously, because it was my position that if Yugoslavia does break down, then the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain within the Serb state. That is my position. And what I say here very expressly is that the Muslims will enjoy full equality, but there is no place for any fundamentalist option. Those who are fundamentalists will have to seek for better conditions in which to do so because fundamentalists, as the most aggressive form of Islam, are engaging in terror throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is whatever it was, 1991 and fundamental -- fundamental Muslims aren't inevitably associated with unlawful violence initiated by foreign countries. Where would you be telling the fundamentalist Muslim hearing this that he had to pack his bags and depart for?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, quite simply, is not true, what you're just saying just now. Fundamentalism at that time was highly topical in the world. It was ten years after the establishment of fundamentalist power in Iran, and I assume you know how far the Iranian fingers were involved in the Bosnian pie and how many fundamentalists from Bosnia received financial aid and all other types of aid from Iran. And secondly, my struggle against Islamic fundamentalism began ten years prior to this, ten years earlier on, and that's why my books were banned, that's why I was sent to prison and arrested, but my struggle and fight did not cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've given the witness enough opportunities to answer that question. The last extract from this document, please, on the next sheet, I expect. Remember I asked you earlier what was a Ustasha. The magazine asked you a question: "Can one reach a solution with cool heads and with rifles laid down?" And you answered this: "How is one supposed to negotiate with the Ustashas? Did you see today that the Croatian people are entirely Ustasha? There are very few exceptions." Can you just explain your answer to that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you read on this text? Feel free. "I pay tribute to the residents of Istria, Rijeka and Kvarner. They are behaving honourably in this situation, and they are not in any kind of danger from the Serbs. That should always be emphasised as an example." Because in Istria, Rijeka, and Kvarner the atmosphere was very tolerant and there were very few cases of Serb persecution. In all other parts of Croatia Tudjman's terror over the Serbs was already raging, but you are taking things out of historical context. "The Ustashas who have gone crazy, we shall defeat them in no time. I guarantee you, with one division of 10.000 Chetniks, we would reach Zagreb within 24 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 48 hours, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer starts with the words that they are not in any kind of danger. The microphone was not on. The beginning of Mr. Seselj's answer was not interpreted at all. Only the second part was interpreted, that they were in no danger. "From certificates." I don't know what this means, I'm reading it out now, and then Rijeka is referred to. So there is no interpretation and this is quite confusing, what it says in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the whole answer was interpreted from the first word on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He started his answer with the following words: "I pay tribute to the citizens or the residents of" et cetera, et cetera, and then he explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in Istria, Rijeka, and Kvarner, in the territories of then Croatia, there was no organised persecution of the Serb population, and that is precisely where the real Croats live, in Istria, Rijeka, Kvarner. That is the Chakavian region, and that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See, on the previous page we've seen the way you've effectively identified those who can stay as those who become loyal citizens of Serbia. Incidentally, would fundamentalists who wanted an independent Bosnia be those who would have to pack their bags and leave?
